newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Commission to propose wider worker consultation.
newsitem.headline: Commission to propose wider worker consultation.

text.p: The European Commission is expected on Wednesday to announce it will ask trades unions and employers to consider negotiating rules obliging national firms in the EU to set up systems for consulting their workers.

The initiative would complement the European Union Works Council directive, 94/45/EC, which already obliges multinational companies to set up procedures for informing and consulting employees about important developments.
Social Affairs Commissioner Padraig Flynn hopes to get approval for the initiative from fellow Commissioners at their regular Wednesday meeting, Commission spokeswoman Barbara Nolan told Reuters.

Flynn will ask the so-called social partners -- representatives of unions and employers -- to tell him within two months whether they want the Commission to propose specific action at European level, Nolan said.

He decided to step up action after the controversial decision by car-maker Renault to shut its assembly plant in Vilvoorde, Belgium, with the loss of 3,100 jobs, revealed gaps in existing legislation, Nolan said.
For one thing, sanctions against companies who failed to consult their employees before taking major restructuring decisions were "derisory" and no real deterrent, she said.

Trades unions representatives have also said existing EU law is not specific enough about the stage at which workers should be consulted and how much influence they should be allowed to have over any company decisions.
Most EU member states have some form of worker consultation system, either enshrined in legislation or in the form of a collective agreement between workers and bosses.
Britain and Ireland have no system at all.

"Our preferred solution would be for the social partners to negotiate a collective agreement at European level because we think they are in the best situation to judge what's happening in the workplace," Nolan said.
Another alternative would be for the EU to bring in a legally-binding directive which would force national companies to set up Works Councils.
Flynn also intends to push ahead with proposals to extend the EU's working time directive, 93/104/EC, to sectors not currently covered -- transport, sea work and doctors in training.
The Commission should publish a white paper, or consultation document, on the subject before the end of June, Nolan said.

Britain's former Conservative government resisted applying the working time directive, which sets a 48-hour maximum working week, but was ordered to comply by the European Court of Justice last November.
